1:1: Παῦλος, καὶ Σιλουανὸς, καὶ Τιμόθεος; τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ
Paul is the author of this letter. Silvanus and Timothy are with him as he writes and are in agreement with what he writes.
The name Silvanus is a longer form of the name Silas, the form of the name used for this same man in the book of Acts.
ἐν Θεῷ Πατρὶ καὶ Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ to describe the union of believers with God and Christ. In this case, being in God and Christ, or united to God and Christ, identifies the Thessalonians as Christians.
Θεῷ Πατρὶ καὶ Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ
When God is called Father, it highlights his relationship to Jesus the “Son” (see 1:10). Here, the Old Testament title for God, Lord, is applied to Jesus, equating him with God.
After stating his name and the people to whom he is writing, Paul adds a blessing.
Many ancient manuscripts read Grace to you and peace.
1:2: Paul says always and continually here as generalizations for emphasis.
1:3: Here, when Paul says that he and those with him are remembering things before our God and Father, he means that they are thanking God about specific things.
Here, our God and Father refers to the one divine person who is both God and Father. The word God and the word Father refer to the same person.
1:4: Here and throughout the letter, Paul uses the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
1:5: τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐγενήθη εἰς ὑμᾶς
Here, Paul speaks of our gospel as if it were a person who could come to you. He means that the Thessalonians heard the gospel from Paul and his fellow workers.
Paul is using the term word to refer to speaking words.

Here Paul could mean that: (1) Paul and those with him preached the gospel with power and with the help of the Holy Spirit and with much assurance that what they preached was true; (2) the Thessalonians experienced power and the Holy Spirit and much assurance when they heard the gospel.

Here, the phrase just as you know could introduce: (1) a basis for Paul’s claim about how the Thessalonians experienced the gospel; (2) a comparison between what Paul has said about how the Thessalonians experienced the gospel and what the Thessalonians know about Paul and his fellow workers.
1:6: Here, the word represents a message that is made up of words, specifically the gospel.
1:7: ἐν τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ καὶ ἐν τῇ Ἀχαΐᾳ
The word Achaia is the name of a Roman province in the southern part of modern-day Greece. The word Macedonia is the same of a Roman province in the northern part of modern-day Greece.
1:8: Paul is using the term word to refer to the message about the Lord, which is the gospel.

Here, Paul speaks as if the Thessalonians were playing an instrument that makes a sound that can be heard from far away. He means that people in many places hear the word of the Lord because of how the Thessalonians act.
Here Paul speaks as if the Thessalonians’ faith were a person who could travel to many places. He means that people in many places have heard about their faith.
Here, the word faith represents knowledge about the Thessalonians’ faith.

Here Paul speaks as if people in every place know about Thessalonians’ faith. The Thessalonians would have understood him to mean that their faith is known in many places, or in every place that Paul and his fellow workers visit.
Here Paul implies that he does not need to say anything about the Thessalonians’ faith.
1:9: Here Paul refers to his and his fellow workers’ visit to the Thessalonians as an entrance. He implies that the Thessalonians welcomed him and that it was a good visit.
ἐπεστρέψατε πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων
Paul speaks of the Thessalonians as if they had been facing toward their idols and then turned around to face toward God. He means that they no longer worship idols, and now they worship God.

Here, the phrase living and true God identifies God as the one who lives and is truly God. The point is that God actually lives, unlike idols and other things that people may call gods, and that God really is God.
1:10: Son is an important title for Jesus that describes his relationship to God the Father.
Here Paul assumes that the Thessalonians know that Jesus ascended into the heavens and will someday come back to earth from there.
Here, the phrase raised from the dead refers to someone who died and came back to life.

Paul speaks of wrath as though it were someone who could travel and is coming to where people are. He means that in the future God will act wrathfully against people who have sinned and who have not trusted in Jesus to forgive their sins.
2:1: τὴν εἴσοδον ἡμῶν τὴν πρὸς ὑμᾶς
Here, just as in 1:9, Paul refers to his and his fellow workers’ visit to the Thessalonians as an entrance.
Paul is using a figure of speech here that expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, not, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning, in vain.
2:2: προπαθόντες καὶ ὑβρισθέντες, καθὼς οἴδατε, ἐν Φιλίπποις
These words provide background information about what happened when Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy were in the city of Philippi.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize how much the apostles suffered.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in God to describe the union of believers with God. In this case, being in God, or united to God, explains how Paul and his fellow workers were able to be bold. Paul could mean more specifically that: (1) God enabled them to be bold; (2) they were bold because of their union with God.
Here, the phrase much struggle could refer: (1) generally to how difficult preaching the gospel was; (2) specifically to people who opposed Paul.
2:3: Here Paul could be implying that this exhortation was addressed to: (1) the Thessalonians specifically; (2) anyone to whom Paul and his fellow workers proclaim the gospel.

Here Paul could be implying that the exhortation was not from error because: (1) he and his fellow workers did not try to convince the Thessalonians to believe what is wrong; (2) he and his fellow workers did not believe what is wrong.
2:4: In Paul’s culture, the heart is the place where humans think and plan.
2:5: Here, the phrase at that time refers to the time when Paul and his fellow workers visited the Thessalonians.
Paul is using the term word to mean a message in words.
The phrase God {is} witness is an oath formula.
2:7: Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers could have made the Thessalonians carry something heavy. He means that he and his fellow workers could have made the Thessalonians’ lives harder. More specifically, the burden could be: (1) Paul and his fellow workers demanding respect and obedience; (2) Paul and his fellow workers demanding money and other things.
Here, Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers became little children. He means that they treated the Thessalonians gently and did not use their authority harshly.
Here, many ancient manuscripts read little children.
ὡς ἐὰν τροφὸς θάλπῃ τὰ ἑαυτῆς τέκνα
The point of this comparison is that in the same way a mother would gently comfort her own children, so the apostles gently and affectionately cared for the Thessalonians.
2:8: Here, the phrase in this manner could: (1) refer back to what Paul said in the previous verse about how he and his fellow workers love and care for the Thessalonians as if they were the Thessalonians’ mothers; (2) make the word longing stronger; (3) refer ahead to what Paul and his fellow workers did because of their longing.
Here, the word souls represents people and focuses particularly on who people are and what they do.
2:9: τὸν κόπον ἡμῶν καὶ τὸν μόχθον
Here, labor and toil mean basically the same thing. The repetition emphasizes how hard the apostles worked.
Here, the phrase night and day indicates that Paul and his fellow workers worked during both the day and the night. This means that they worked very much every day.
πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαί τινα ὑμῶν
Here Paul speaks of asking for money as if it were a heavy burden that he and his fellow workers could have asked the Thessalonians to carry for them.
2:10: ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες καὶ ὁ Θεός, ὡς

Here Paul speaks as if he were summoning both the Thessalonians and God as witnesses to testify on their behalf before a judge. He means that both the Thessalonians and God know how he and his fellow workers acted.
ὡς ὁσίως, καὶ δικαίως, καὶ ἀμέμπτως
The terms piously, righteously, and blamelessly mean similar things. Paul is using the three terms together for emphasis.
2:11: The point of Paul’s comparison is that Paul and his fellow workers are like fathers who model and instruct proper behavior for their children.
2:12: παρακαλοῦντες ὑμᾶς, καὶ παραμυθούμενοι, καὶ μαρτυρόμενοι
Here, the words exhorting, encouraging, and testifying describe ways in which Paul and his fellow workers acted like fathers.
The terms exhorting and encouraging mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Paul could be implying that he and his fellow workers testify: (1) about how believers should behave; (2) to the truth of the good news.
Paul speaks of behavior in life as if it were walking.
εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ βασιλείαν καὶ δόξαν

Here, the phrase kingdom and glory could refer: (1) to two distinct things that God calls his people to participate in; (2) to one thing described with two words connected by and. This is called hendiadys.
2:13: Here, the word also could imply that: (1) Paul and his fellow workers thank God about the Thessalonians like other people do (see 1:8–10); (2) Paul and his fellow workers are thanking God for additional things about the Thessalonians.
Paul says continually here as a generalization for emphasis.
λόγον ἀκοῆς … λόγον ἀνθρώπων … λόγον Θεοῦ
In this verse, Paul uses the term word to mean a message that is spoken by using words.
Here Paul refers to the word of God as if it were a person doing work. He means that God uses the word to work in the Thessalonians.
2:14: Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ Jesus. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ, explains that churches are truly believers and have a relationship with Christ.

Here Paul is referring to Jewish people who did not believe in Jesus and who persecuted those who did believe in Jesus. He is not referring to Jewish people in general, since the churches of God that are in Judea were mostly Jewish people.
2:15: Paul provides this background information about “the Jews” to help readers understand exactly which Jews he is speaking about.
This list of those persecuted by the people whom Paul calls “the Jews” is not chronological but emphasizes the order of importance and intensity of persecution.
Here, the phrase the prophets refers to the prophets who are mentioned in the Old Testament. These prophets were also Jewish and spoke God’s message to his people.
Paul says all men here as a generalization for emphasis.
2:16: Here Paul implies that he and his fellow workers speaks the gospel.
εἰς τὸ ἀναπληρῶσαι αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας πάντοτε
Here Paul is referring to how the unbelieving Jews fill up their sins. He does not mean that the Gentiles who are saved are filling up their sins.
εἰς τὸ ἀναπληρῶσαι αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας πάντοτε

Here, Paul speaks of how the unbelieving Jews sin as if it were filling something up with sins. He could mean: (1) that they commit many sins all the time; (2) that they commit enough sins that God will punish them.
Here Paul implies that the wrath is God’s wrath.

Here, the phrase to the end could mean that God’s wrath has come up them: (1) completely or totally. In this case, God reveals all of his wrath, not just some of it; (2) at a specific moment at the end of a period of time. In this case, the unbelieving Jews are sinning until God finally reveals his wrath; (3) at the end of this world. In this case, the end refers to when Jesus comes back.
2:17: Here Paul refers to how he and his fellow workers had to leave the Thessalonians soon after arriving in their city and preaching the good news to them.
Here, the phrase for the time of an hour refers to a short span of time.

Here, the word face represents physical presence, and the word heart represents thoughts and desires. Paul means that he and his fellow workers thought and cared about the Thessalonians (by heart) even though they were not physically present in Thessalonica (by face).
The terms extremely eager and in much desire mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The phrase to see your face refers to visiting someone and being with them.
2:18: Here, the phrase both once and twice could mean that: (1) Paul tried to visit the Thessalonians multiple times. In this case, Paul does not clarify how many times he tried; (2) Paul tried to visit them twice.
Here Paul means that Satan prevented him and his fellow workers from visiting the Thessalonians.
2:19: Paul is using the question form to show the Thessalonians how much he and his fellow workers value and care about them.
In the next question, Paul identifies the hope, joy, and crown as the Thessalonians themselves.
Here, Paul speaks of the honor and recognition that someone receives for accomplishing a task or goal as if it were a crown.
Here, many ancient manuscripts read of boasting.

Here, the phrase before our Lord Jesus implies that Paul, his fellow workers, and the Thessalonians will be examined by the Lord Jesus. Paul is confident that Jesus will approve of the Thessalonians, which will give Paul and his fellow workers honor and joy.
Here, the phrase his coming refers to the specific time in the future when Jesus will come back to earth, judge everyone, punish unbelievers, and reward believers.
3:1: Here Paul implies that he and his fellow workers could no longer endure being separated from the Thessalonians and longing to see them.
The word Athens is the name of a city. It was one of the most important cities in the country we call Greece.
3:2: Here Paul implies that he and Silvanus sent Timothy to visit the Thessalonians.
Paul is using the term brother to mean a person who shares the same faith with him.
Many ancient manuscripts read a servant of God.
The preposition in could refer to: (1) how Timothy works to preach the gospel; (2) the means by which Timothy serves.
Here, Paul is speaking of Timothy supporting or helping the Thessalonians in their faith as if he were making them physically stronger.
3:4: Here Paul means that what he and his fellow workers told the Thessalonians would happen did indeed happen, and the Thessalonians know it.
3:5: Here, much as in 3:1 Paul implies that he could no longer endure being separated from the Thessalonians and not knowing how they were doing.
Here Paul implies that he sent Timothy to the Thessalonians.
Here, the phrase lest somehow introduces something that Paul was worried about.
Here Paul uses the phrase the tempter to refer to the devil, Satan.
Here Paul implies that he was worried not only that they would be tempted but also that they would stop believing when they were tempted.
Here, the phrase in vain identifies a cause that does not have its intended effect. In this case, Paul’s labor will not help the Thessalonians if the tempter successfully tempts them.
3:6: Here, the clause you always have good memory of us indicates that the Thessalonians remembered Paul and his fellow workers as people whom they liked and would want to meet again.
Here, the word longing could introduce: (1) another thing that the Thessalonians do.
3:7: Here, the phrase translated about you could identify: (1) what Paul and his fellow workers are encouraged about; (2) the reason why Paul and his fellow workers are encouraged.
ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ ἀνάγκῃ καὶ θλίψει ἡμῶν
The terms distress and affliction mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:8: Here, the word now could refer to: (1) the time when Paul and his fellow workers live; (2) the result of how the Thessalonians stand firm.
Here, the phrase we live means that Paul and his fellow workers are refreshed and able to enjoy their lives. Paul does not mean that they were dead or about to die and are now alive again.
Here, the phrase stand firm in indicates that people are remaining faithful to whomever they are in.
3:9: τίνα … εὐχαριστίαν δυνάμεθα τῷ Θεῷ ἀνταποδοῦναι

Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers owe God a debt that they can pay back by giving thanks. He means that the appropriate response to God’s work among the Thessalonians is to give thanks to God.
Many ancient manuscripts read to God and our God.
ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ χαρᾷ ᾗ χαίρομεν
Here Paul uses both the word joy and the word rejoice to emphasize how much joy he and his fellow workers have.
Here, the phrase before our God means that Paul and his fellow workers rejoice in God’s presence.
3:10: Here, the phrase night and day indicates that Paul and his fellow workers were pleading earnestly during both the day and the night. This means that they were pleading earnestly very often every day.
Here Paul implies that he and his fellow workers pray to God when they are pleading.
εἰς τὸ ἰδεῖν ὑμῶν τὸ πρόσωπον
The phrase to see your face refers to visiting someone and being with them.
καταρτίσαι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν
Here Paul could be implying that the Thessalonians are lacking: (1) knowledge about God that should be included in their faith; (2) some aspects of faith in God.
3:11: Paul speaks about God the Father and the Lord Jesus as if they were directing Paul’s way and his fellow worker’s ways. He could mean that God the Father and the Lord Jesus: (1) are like guides who take Paul and his fellow workers to meet the Thessalonians, which would enable Paul and his fellow workers to visit the Thessalonians; (2) enable Paul and his fellow workers to overcome obstacles that prevent them from visiting the Thessalonians; (3) lead Paul and his fellow workers on a straight path to the Thessalonians, which would enable Paul and his fellow workers to visit the Thessalonians soon.
Here, the phrase our God and Father refers to the one divine person who is both God and Father. The word God and the word Father refer to the same person.
3:12: ὑμᾶς … ὁ Κύριος πλεονάσαι καὶ περισσεύσαι
The terms increase and abound mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:13: εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας
Here Paul speaks of the Thessalonians becoming spiritually stronger as if their hearts were being strengthened.
ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν

Here, the phrase before our God and Father refers to being in the presence of our God and Father. In this case, the phrase emphasizes that God is the one who will declare the Thessalonians to be blameless in holiness.
Here, the phrase our God and Father refers to the one divine person who is both God and Father. The word God and the word Father refer to the same person.
ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ
Here, the phrase the coming of our Lord Jesus refers to the specific time in the future when Jesus will come back to earth, judge everyone, punish unbelievers, and reward believers.
Here, the word saints could refer to: (1) believers; (2) believers and angels; (3) angels.
4:1: The terms ask and encourage mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in the Lord Jesus to describe the union of believers with Jesus. In this case, being in the Lord Jesus, or united to Jesus, could specifically explain: (1) the reason why Paul and his fellow workers ask and exhort the Thessalonians; (2) the authority by which Paul and his fellow workers ask and exhort the Thessalonians.
Paul speaks of behavior in life as if it were walking.
Here, to walk and to please expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word please describes the way in which the Thessalonian church should walk.
Here Paul implies that he and his fellow workers want the Thessalonians to abound even more in pleasing God.
4:2: Here Paul refers to what he and his fellow workers told the Thessalonians when they first visited them.
Here, the phrase through the Lord Jesus indicates that Paul and his fellow workers said what the Lord Jesus wanted them to say. In other words, they spoke with the authority of the Lord Jesus.
4:3: Here, the phrase that you keep yourselves introduces an explanation of what Paul means when he uses the word sanctification. This explanation continues in 4:4–6.
4:4: Here, the phrase that each of you knows could: (1) give another example of what “sanctification” means (See: 4:3); (2) describe more specifically what it means to avoid “sexual immorality” (See: 4:3).
Here, the word knows could refer specifically to: (1) learning how to do something; (2) understanding something.
Here, the word vessel could refer to: (1) a person’s sexual organ. This is a euphemism; (2) a man’s wife. This is a metaphor.

The meaning of the verb possess depends on what the word vessel means (See: the previous note): (1) If the word vessel refers to the body or more specifically to the sexual organ, the word possess refers to people having control over their bodies; (2) If the word vessel refers to a wife, the word possess could refer to a man having sex with his wife; (3) If the word vessel refers to a wife, the word possess could refer to a man marrying a woman.
4:5: Here, the phrase not knowing God means that these Gentiles do not listen to, trust in, or obey God. It does not mean that they do not know about God.
4:6: The two terms transgress and take advantage of work together to express a single idea. The phrase take advantage of tells how a person might transgress.
Paul is using the term brother to mean a person who shares the same faith.
Here, the phrase this matter refers to what Paul has been speaking about: sexual morality.
καθὼς καὶ προείπαμεν ὑμῖν καὶ διεμαρτυράμεθα
Here Paul refers to what he and his fellow workers told the Thessalonians when they visited them.
The terms said before and testified mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
4:8: Many ancient manuscripts read the one giving.
4:9: Here Paul uses the phrase brotherly love to refer to love for people who share the same faith, both men and women.
4:10: Here Paul implies that he and his fellow workers want the Thessalonians to abound in brotherly love even more.
4:11: Here, the phrase to be quiet refers to living in a peaceful way that does not disrupt others.
Here, the phrase to perform your own things refers to focusing on one’s own tasks and responsibilities instead of becoming involved in other people’s private affairs.

Here Paul uses the phrase work with your own hands to indicate that the Thessalonians should support themselves instead of relying on others to provide for them. He does not mean that they must do physical labor.
Here Paul refers to what he and his fellow workers commanded the Thessalonians when they visited them.
4:12: Paul speaks of behavior in life as if it were walking.
Here, the phrase the ones outside identifies people who do not belong to the group of believers in Thessalonica.

Here word translated nothing could refer: (1) to things. In this case, Paul wants them to have everything that they need; (2) to people. In this case, Paul wants them to be independent and not rely on other people to provide for them.
4:13: Here, the phrase the ones sleeping is a polite way to refer to people who have died.
Here Paul implies that the hope concerns what happens to people after they die. People who do not have hope do not expect anyone who dies to live again.
4:14: Here, the word rose refers to how Jesus came back to life after he died.

Here Paul does not explicitly state all the elements in his comparison between Jesus and the the ones having slept. He states that Jesus died and rose, and he implies that this will be true for the ones having slept. He states that the ones having slept will be brought with Jesus, and he implies that Jesus is coming back to this world.

Here, the phrase will bring could mean that: (1) God will send resurrected believers with Jesus when Jesus comes back to this world; (2) God will bring resurrected believers to be with Jesus in heaven.
4:15: Paul is using the term word to mean a message that is shared by using words.
Here, the phrase the coming of the Lord refers to the specific time in the future when Jesus will come back to earth, judge everyone, punish unbelievers, and reward believers.

Here, the phrase will certainly not go before indicates that people who are alive when Jesus comes back will not meet him first. Instead, believers who have died will meet him first, and then believers who are alive will meet him. Paul explains this further in the following verse (see 4:16).
4:16: Here Paul does not specify who gives the loud command. He implies that it is God.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, indicates that Paul is speaking only about the dead who are united to Christ, that is, believers.
Here, the word rise refers to people who had died then coming back to life.

Here, the word first indicates that, after Jesus comes down from heaven, the dead in Christ will resurrect before anything else happens. Paul indicates in the following verse what happens after they resurrect.
4:17: Here, the phrase in the clouds could refer to: (1) the place where believers meet the Lord. In other words, the clouds are in the air, which is where believers meet the Lord; (2) the means by which believers go to meet the Lord. In this case, the clouds are what believers stand on as they go to meet the Lord. Some people in Paul’s culture told stories about people standing on clouds as they traveled to heaven.
εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα

Here, the phrase to meet refers to going to greet someone. Paul could be implying that, after believers greet him, Jesus: (1) continues to earth with all believers; (2) goes back up to heaven with all believers, either temporarily or eternally.
Here, the phrase in the air refers to the area above the earth but below heaven, an area often called the sky.
Here, the phrase in this way refers to the process that Paul has outlined in this verse and the previous verse.
4:18: Here, the phrase these words refers to what Paul has said in 4:13–17.
5:1: Here Paul implies that the times and the seasons relate to questions concerning when Jesus will come back. In other words, Paul has begun to talk about the timing of Jesus’ second coming.
The terms times and seasons mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together to refer in general to the timing of Jesus’ second coming.
5:2: Here, Paul speaks of the day of the Lord as if it were a person who could come to a place. He means that the event named the day of the Lord will happen.
ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ οὕτως ἔρχεται
Paul is saying that the day of the Lord is like a thief in the night because people cannot tell when either one will happen.
5:3: Here, the word destruction refers to severe suffering or punishment. It does not mean that they people who experience the destruction cease to exist.
Paul is saying that sudden destruction during the day of the Lord is like birth pain because both events begin suddenly and cannot be avoided.
Here, the phrase the one having in the womb refers to a woman who is pregnant.
5:4: Here Paul speaks as if the Thessalonians are not in a place that has no light. He could mean that: (1) they are not ignorant about the day of the Lord; (2) they are not avoiding and disobeying God.
Here, Paul speaks of the day as if it were a person who could overtake the Thessalonians. He means that the event named the day will not surprise or shock the Thessalonians.
ἡ ἡμέρα ὑμᾶς ὡς κλέπτας καταλάβῃ
Paul is saying that the day of the Lord will overtake some people as sunshine overtakes thieves because both the people and the thieves are surprised by and unprepared for the day to arrive.
Here Paul is again referring to what he called “the day of the Lord” in 5:2.

Here, many ancient manuscripts read as thieves. Other ancient manuscripts read “as a thief.” This reading would mean that the day overtakes some people as a thief overtakes people and steals from them.
5:5: Here, the phrases sons of the light and sons of day mean basically the same thing. Also, the phrases of night and of darkness mean basically the same thing. Paul is using these phrases together for emphasis.

The expression son of describes a person who shares the qualities of something. Paul is using this expression to describe the behavior and character of the Thessalonians, since they are people who are characterized by light and day.
Here Paul speaks of the Thessalonians as if they were characterized by light and day (see the previous note for the meaning of the phrase son of). He means that they obey God and do what is right.

Here Paul speaks of believers as those who are not characterized by night and darkness (see the previous note for the meaning of the phrases of night and of darkness). He means that believers are not people who disobey God and do what is wrong.
5:6: Here Paul speaks about the people “of the night” and “of the darkness” as if they were sleeping. He means that they are unaware of or unprepared for the Lord’s return because they are living sinfully.

Here, Paul speaks as if believers were guards who needed to keep watch and be sober. He means that believers should be aware of and prepared for the Lord’s return, and they should be self-controlled so that they live in a way that pleases God.
5:7: Here Paul provides two parallel examples of what people do at night. He repeats the same structure and the phrase at night in both clauses, which emphasizes at night.
Here Paul provides common examples of what people sometimes do during the night. He is not using sleeping and getting drunk to speak about something else.
5:8: Here, the phrase of day means basically the same thing as the phrase “sons of day” in 5:5. Paul means that believers obey God and do what is right, just as people usually do what is right during the day.

Here, the phrase be sober contrasts with the phrase “get drunk” in the previous verse (5:7). Paul means that believers should be self-controlled and obedient to God. He does not just mean that they should not get drunk, although that is part of the command.

Here Paul speaks of Christians acting in faith and love as if each of them were a soldier putting on a breastplate. He speaks of Christians experiencing the hope of salvation as if each of them were a soldier putting on a helmet. He means that faith, love, and hope protect believers, just as armor protects soldiers. Paul does not directly state what believers are protected from, but he implies that it is sin and evil powers, including the devil.
A helmet is a strong hat that a soldier would wear to protect his or her head.
5:9: Here, the word wrath refers to how God will punish people who do not believe and who disobey him. This punishment will occur during “the day of the Lord” that Paul has already mentioned.
5:10: Here, the phrase for us could indicate that Jesus died: (1) to benefit or help us; (2) instead of or in place of us.

Here Paul could be using the terms keep watch and sleep to refer to: (1) being alive and being dead; (2) waiting expectantly for Jesus to return and being dead; (3) doing what pleases God and not doing what pleases God.
5:11: παρακαλεῖτε ἀλλήλους, καὶ οἰκοδομεῖτε εἷς τὸν ἕνα
The commands encourage one another and build up one the one mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, Paul is speaking of the Thessalonian believers as if they were a building.
Here, the phrase one the one indicates that each person should be building up each other person.
Here Paul means that the Thessalonians are already doing what he is asking them to do.
5:12: Here Paul could be using these three phrases: (1) to refer to three distinct activities; (2) to refer to one primary activity (laboring) that he defines as leading and admonishing.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in the Lord to describe the union of believers with the Lord. In this case, being in the Lord, or united to Christ, could: (1) identify the leaders as those who lead people who believe in Christ; (2) indicate that the Lord has authorized these leaders.
5:13: Here, the phrase in love could give: (1) the context in which the Thessalonians should regard them highly. In other words, the Thessalonians should regard them highly while they are loving them; (2) the manner in which the Thessalonians should regard them highly.
Here, the phrase regard them highly means that the Thessalonians should greatly respect and honor their leaders in the church.
5:14: Here, the word disorderly could describe: (1) people who live in undisciplined and disruptive ways; (2) people who refuse to work to support themselves.
Here, the word all could refer to: (1) people in general; (2) just believers.
5:15: Here Paul tells the Thessalonians to see or look at what he wants them to do.
Here Paul means that the Thessalonians should not do what is evil to people who have done what is evil. In other words, when someone treats them badly, they should not respond in the same way.

Here Paul speaks as if he wants the Corinthians to run after and try to capture {what is} good. He speaks in this way because he wants them to do {what is} good as persistently as someone who pursues someone or something.
καὶ εἰς ἀλλήλους καὶ εἰς πάντας
Here, the phrase one another refers to the believers in Thessalonica. The word all refers to all people, whether they are believers or not.
5:17: Paul says continually here as a generalization for emphasis.
5:18: Here, the phrase In everything could refer to: (1) every situation or experience; (2) every moment in time.
θέλημα Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς

Here Paul could mean: (1) that the will of God has been revealed in Christ Jesus; (2) that the will of God is for people who are in Christ Jesus. In other words, these commands are what God wants people who are in union with Christ Jesus to do.
5:19: Paul speaks of the Holy Spirit as if he were a fire that the Thessalonians should not quench. Paul means that the Thessalonians should not hinder or oppose the work of the Holy Spirit.
5:20: Paul is using a figure of speech here that expresses a strongly positive meaning by using a negative word, not, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning, despise.
5:21: Here, many ancient manuscripts read Test all things.

Here Paul could be referring to: (1) the “prophecies” that he referred to in the previous verse (see 5:20); (2) spiritual gifts, or how the Holy Spirit specially empowers each person; (3) anything people say and do.
Here Paul speaks as if what {is} good were an object that the Thessalonians could grasp tightly. He means that they should believe and act based on whatever is good.
5:22: Here, much as in the previous verse (5:22), Paul could be referring to: (1) the “prophecies” that he referred to in 5:20; (2) spiritual gifts, or how the Holy Spirit specially empowers each person; (3) anything people say and do.
Here, the word translated form could refer to: (1) a type or kind of something; (2) the way that something looks or appears.
5:23: Here Paul is asking God to bless the Thessalonians.

Here Paul uses the three terms spirit, soul, and body together to refer to the whole person. These three terms could: (1) describe different aspects of the whole person from different perspectives. In this case, the three terms do not define three separate pieces that together make up a person.
Here, the word blamelessly could refer to: (1) the situation in which the spirit, soul, and body are kept; (2) the result of the spirit, soul, and body being kept.
ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Here, the phrase the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ refers to the specific time in the future when Jesus will come back to earth, judge everyone, punish unbelievers, and reward believers.
5:24: Here Paul does not state directly what God will do. He implies that God will do what Paul prayed for in the previous verse (see 5:23).
5:25: Here, also indicates that the Thessalonians should be praying for Paul, Silas, and Timothy just as Paul, Silas, and Timothy pray for them (see 5:23).
5:26: A holy kiss was a symbolic action to show familial love between believers. In some cultures, a kiss as a greeting is appropriate, but in other cultures it is not appropriate. The idea of a holy kiss is that it be a greeting that is appropriate in the culture, whether it be a kiss, a hug, a handshake, or something else, and also that it be holy, that is, appropriate between God’s people.
5:27: The phrase {by} the Lord could be: (1) an oath formula.
In Paul’s culture, letters sent to a group were normally read out loud by one person to everyone else in the group.
Many ancient manuscripts read all the brothers.
5:28: As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for the Thessalonians.
Here, the word our includes Paul, Silvanus, Timothy, the Thessalonians, and all believers.
Here, many ancient manuscripts read {be} with you. Other ancient manuscripts add “Amen” after {be} with you.
